title.en: The Making of a Global World
A cup of tea from far away

text.en: The tea in your cup, the potato on your plate and even your phone depend on trade that links continents. Today we trace how the world became connected.

Early trade linked Asia, Europe and Africa through the Silk Routes, which also carried ideas, religions and diseases.
After Europeans reached the Americas, food crops such as potato, maize and tomato spread across the world, and disease devastated the native peoples.
In the nineteenth century the abolition of the Corn Laws in Britain in 1846 made food imports cheaper and shifted agriculture overseas.
Rinderpest, a cattle plague, spread across Africa in the 1890s and destroyed cattle, which weakened local people and helped colonial control.
Indentured labour carried Indian workers to plantations in the Caribbean, Fiji and Mauritius under harsh contracts.
The First World War and then the Great Depression from 1929 caused unemployment, falling prices and the collapse of banks.
In 1944 the Bretton Woods conference set up the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to keep the economy stable.
After 1950s, former colonies formed the Group of 77 to demand a New International Economic Order, and later multinational companies spread across the world.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking it affected only the USA

points.en: The Silk Routes linked continents early.
Corn Laws and Rinderpest changed economies in the 19th century.
Bretton Woods created the IMF and World Bank.
